The '''ratio of uniforms''' is a method initially proposed by Kinderman and Monahan in 1977<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kinderman|first1=A. J.|last2=Monahan|first2=J. F.|date=September 1977|title=Computer Generation of Random Variables Using the Ratio of Uniform Deviates|journal=ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software|volume=3|issue=3|pages=257–260|doi=10.1145/355744.355750|s2cid=12884505|doi-access=free}}</ref> for [[pseudo-random number sampling]], that is, for drawing random samples from a [[statistical distribution]]. Like [[rejection sampling]] and [[inverse transform sampling]], it is an exact simulation method. The basic idea of the method is to use a change of variables to create a bounded set, which can then be sampled uniformly to generate random variables following the original distribution. One feature of this method is that the distribution to sample is only required to be known up to an unknown multiplicative factor, a common situation in computational statistics and statistical physics.

== Motivation ==

[[File:Rejection_sampling_of_a_bounded_distribution_with_finite_support.svg|alt=The pdf of a bimodal statistical distribution is plotted on a graph. The distribution is only defined between −1.5 and 1.5. A rectangular bounding box is drawn around the graph of the function between the abscisses −1.5 and 1.5, and the y coordinates 0 and the maximum of the function. The box is split into two zones by the curve: below the curve is the acceptance region, and above it is the rejection region.|thumb|317x317px|Rejection sampling of a bounded statistical distribution with finite support.]]

A convenient technique to sample a statistical distribution is [[rejection sampling]].  When the [[probability density function]] of the distribution is bounded and has finite [[support of a distribution|support]], one can define a bounding box around it (a uniform proposal distribution), draw uniform samples in the box and return only the x coordinates of the points that fall below the function (see graph).  As a direct consequence of the [[fundamental theorem of simulation]],<ref name="Robert2004MonteCarlo">{{cite book |last1=Robert |first1=Christian |last2=Casella |first2=George |title=Monte Carlo Statistical Methods |date=2004 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |isbn=978-0-387-21239-5 |page=47 |edition=2 |url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9780387212395 |language=en}}</ref> the returned samples are distributed according to the original distribution.

When the support of the distribution is infinite, it is impossible to draw a rectangular bounding box containing the graph of the function.  One can still use [[rejection sampling]], but with a non-uniform proposal distribution.  It can be delicate to choose an appropriate proposal distribution,<ref name="Martino2013Generalized">{{cite arXiv|last1=Martino|first1=Luca|last2=Luengo|first2=David|last3=Míguez|first3=Joaquín|date=16 July 2013|title=On the Generalized Ratio of Uniforms as a Combination of Transformed Rejection and Extended Inverse of Density Sampling|eprint=1205.0482|page=13|class=stat.CO}}</ref> and one also has to know how to efficiently sample this proposal distribution.

The method of the ratio of uniforms offers a solution to this problem, by essentially using as proposal distribution the distribution created by the ratio of two [[Continuous uniform distribution|uniform random variables]].

== Statement ==
The statement and the proof are adapted from the presentation by Gobet<ref>{{Cite book|last=GOBET|first=EMMANUEL|title=MONTE-CARLO METHODS AND STOCHASTIC PROCESSES : from linear to non-linear.|date=2020|publisher=CRC PRESS|isbn=978-0-367-65846-5|location=[S.l.]|oclc=1178639517}}</ref>

{{Math theorem|Let <math>X</math> be a multidimensional [[random variable]] with [[probability density function]] <math>p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d)</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math>. The function <math>p</math> is only required to be known up to a constant, so we can assume that we only know <math>f</math> where <math>p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d) = c f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d)</math>, with <math>c</math> a constant unknown or difficult to compute. Let <math>r>0</math>, a parameter that can be adjusted as we choose to improve the properties of the method. We can define the set <math>A_{f,r}</math>:<math display="block">A_{f,r} = \left\{(u, v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_d) \in \mathbb{R}^{d+1}: 0 \leq u \leq f\left(\frac{v_1}{u^r},\frac{v_2}{u^r}, \ldots,\frac{v_d}{u^r} \right)^{\frac{1}{1+rd}}\right\}</math>The [[Lebesgue measure]] of the set <math>A_{f,r}</math> is finite and equal to <math>\frac{1}{c\,(1+rd)}</math>.

Furthermore, let <math>(U, V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_d)</math> be a random variable uniformly distributed on the set <math>A_{f,r}</math>. Then, <math>\left(\frac{V_1}{U^r}, \frac{V_2}{U^r}, \ldots, \frac{V_d}{U^r}\right)</math> is a random variable on <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math> distributed like <math>X</math>.
}}

{{Math proof|We will first assume that the first statement is correct, i.e. <math>|A_{f,r}| = \frac{1}{c\,(1+rd)}</math>.

Let <math>\varphi</math> be a [[measurable function]] on <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math>. Let's consider the [[Expected value|expectation]] of <math>\varphi\left(\frac{V_1}{U^r}, \ldots, \frac{V_d}{U^r}\right)</math> on the set <math>A_{f,r}</math>:

: <math display="block">E\left[\varphi\left(\frac{V_1}{U^r}, \ldots, \frac{V_d}{U^r}\right)\right]
= \frac{1}{|A_{f,r}|}
\int_{-\infty}^\infty\int_{-\infty}^\infty\cdots\int_{-\infty}^\infty\varphi\left(\frac{v_1}{u^r},\ldots,\frac{v_d}{u^r}\right)\mathbf{1}_{(u, v_1, \ldots, v_d)\in A_{f,r}}\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v_1\ldots\mathrm{d}v_d</math>

With the change of variables <math>x_i = \frac{v_i}{u^r}</math>, we have

: <math>\begin{align}
E\left[\varphi\left(\frac{V_1}{U^r},\ldots,\frac{V_d}{U^r}\right)\right]
&= \frac{1}{|A_{f,r}|}
\int_{-\infty}^\infty\int_{-\infty}^\infty\cdots\int_{-\infty}^\infty
\varphi(x_1,\ldots,x_d)
\mathbf{1}_{0\leq u\leq f(x_1,\ldots, x_d)^\frac{1}{1+rd}}
u^{rd}
\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}x_1\cdots\mathrm{d}x_d\\
&= \frac{1}{|A_{f,r}|}
\int_{-\infty}^\infty\cdots\int_{-\infty}^\infty
\varphi\left(x_1,\ldots,x_d\right)
\frac{1}{1+rd}f\left(x_1,\ldots,x_d\right)
\mathrm{d}x_1\cdots\mathrm{d}x_d\\
&= \int_{-\infty}^\infty\ldots\int_{-\infty}^\infty
\varphi\left(x_1,\ldots,x_d\right)p\left(x_1,\ldots,x_d\right)
\mathrm{d}x_1\cdots\mathrm{d}x_d
\end{align}</math>

where we can see that <math>\left(\frac{V_1}{U^r}, \ldots, \frac{V_d}{U^r}\right)</math> has indeed the density <math>p</math>.

Coming back to the first statement, a similar argument shows that <math>|A_{f,r}| = \frac{1}{c\,(1+rd)}</math>.}}

== Complements ==

=== Rejection sampling in <math>A_{f,r}</math> ===
The above statement does not specify how one should perform the uniform sampling in <math>A_{f,r}</math>. However, the interest of this method is that under mild conditions on <math>f</math> (namely that <math>f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d)^{\frac{1}{1+rd}}</math> and <math>x_i f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d)^\frac{r}{1+rd}</math> for all <math>i</math> are [[Bounded function|bounded]]), <math>A_{f,r}</math> is [[Bounded set|bounded]]. One can define the rectangular bounding box <math>\tilde{A}_{f,r}</math> such that<math display="block">A_{f,r} \subset \tilde{A}_{f,r} = 
\left[0, \sup_{x_1, \ldots, x_d}{f(x_1, \ldots, x_d)^{\frac{1}{1+rd}}}\right]
\times
\prod_i \left[\inf_{x_1, \ldots, x_d}{x_i f(x_1, \ldots, x_d)^{\frac{r}{1+rd}}},
\sup_{x_1, \ldots, x_d}{x_i f(x_1, \ldots, x_d)^{\frac{r}{1+rd}}}\right]</math>This allows to sample uniformly the set <math>A_{f,r}</math> by [[rejection sampling]] inside <math>\tilde{A}_{f,r}</math>. The parameter <math>r</math> can be adjusted to change the shape of <math>A_{f,r}</math> and maximize the acceptance ratio of this sampling.

=== Parametric description of the boundary of <math>A_{f,r}</math> ===
The definition of <math>A_{f,r}</math> is already convenient for the rejection sampling step. For illustration purposes, it can be interesting to draw the set, in which case it can be useful to know the parametric description of its boundary:<math display="block">u = f\left(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d \right)^\frac{1}{1+rd}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\forall i \in [|1, n|], v_i = x_i u^r</math>or for the common case where <math>X</math> is a 1-dimensional variable, <math>(u, v) = \left(f(x)^\frac{1}{1+r}, x\,f(x)^\frac{r}{1+r}\right)</math>.

=== Generalized ratio of uniforms ===

Above parameterized only with <math>r</math>, the ratio of uniforms can be described with a more general class of transformations in terms of a transformation ''g''.<ref name="Wakefield1991Efficient">{{cite journal |last1=Wakefield |first1=J. C. |last2=Gelfand |first2=A. E. |last3=Smith |first3=A. F. M. |title=Efficient generation of random variates via the ratio-of-uniforms method |journal=Statistics and Computing |date=1 December 1991 |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=129–133 |doi=10.1007/BF01889987 |s2cid=119824513 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01889987 |language=en |issn=1573-1375|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In the 1-dimensional case, if <math>g: \mathbb{R}^+\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^+</math> is a strictly increasing and differentiable function such that <math>g(0) = 0</math>, then we can define <math>A_{f,g}</math> such that

: <math display="block">A_{f,g} = \left\{(u, v)\in\mathbb{R}^2: 0\leq u \leq g^{-1}\left[f\left(\frac{v}{g'(u)}\right)\right]\right\}</math>

If <math>(U, V)</math> is a random variable uniformly distributed in <math>A_{f,g}</math>, then <math>\frac{V}{g'(U)}</math> is distributed with the density <math>p</math>.

== Examples ==

[[File:Ratio of uniforms for the exponential distribution.svg|thumb|318x318px|Exponential distribution before and after change of variables by the ratio of uniforms method. Top: graph of the exponential distribution on <math>\mathbb{R}^+</math>. Bottom: the set <math>A_{f,1}</math> is represented in the space <math>(u, v)</math>, inscribed in the bounding box <math>\tilde{A}_{f,1}</math>. The colored domains, of equal probability, were added to help the visual association of the corresponding domains of the transformed sets.]]

=== The exponential distribution ===

Assume that we want to sample the [[exponential distribution]], <math>p(x) = \lambda \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}</math> with the ratio of uniforms method. We will take here <math>r = 1</math>.

We can start constructing the set <math>A_{f,1}</math>:

: <math>A_{f,1} = \left\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^2:0\leq u\leq \sqrt{p\left(\frac{v}{u}\right)} \right\}</math>

The condition <math>0\leq u\leq \sqrt{p\left(\frac{v}{u}\right)}</math> is equivalent, after computation, to <math>0\leq v\leq -\frac{u}{\lambda}\ln\frac{u^2}{\lambda}</math>, which allows us to plot the shape of the set (see graph).

This inequality also allows us to determine the rectangular bounding box <math>\tilde{A}_{f,1}</math> where <math>A_{f,1}</math> is included. Indeed, with <math>g(u) = -\frac{u}{\lambda}\ln\frac{u^2}{\lambda}</math>, we have <math>g\left(\sqrt{\lambda}\right) = 0</math> and <math>g'\left(\frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{\mathrm{e}}\right) = 0</math>, from where <math>\tilde{A}_{f,1} = \left[0, \sqrt{\lambda}\right]\times\left[0, \frac{2}{\mathrm{e}\sqrt{\lambda}}\right]</math>.

From here, we can draw pairs of uniform random variables <math>U \sim \mathrm{Unif}\left(0, \sqrt{\lambda}\right)</math> and <math>V \sim \mathrm{Unif}\left(0, \frac{2}{\mathrm{e}\sqrt{\lambda}}\right)</math> until <math>u \leq \sqrt{\lambda\,\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda\frac{v}{u}}}</math>, and when that happens, we return <math>\frac{v}{u}</math>, which is exponentially distributed.

[[File:Ratio of uniforms for normal mixture distribution.svg|thumb|321x321px|Normal mixture distribution before and after change of variables by the ratio of uniforms method. Top: graph of the mixture distribution on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. Bottom: the set <math>A_{f,r}</math> is represented for two different values of <math>r</math>. The solid lines on the top represent the de-transformation of the bounding boxes on the bottom. The solid lines on the bottom represent the locations of different values of <math>x</math> in the set.]]

=== A mixture of normal distributions ===

Consider the [[Mixture distribution|mixture]] of two [[normal distribution]]s <math>\mathcal{D} = 0.6\,N(\mu=-1, \sigma=2)+0.4\,N(\mu=3, \sigma=1)</math>. To apply the method of the ratio of uniforms, with a given <math>r</math>, one should first determine the boundaries of the rectangular bounding box <math>\tilde{A}_{f,r}</math> enclosing the set <math>A_{f,r}</math>. This can be done numerically, by computing the minimum and maximum of <math>u(x) = f(x)^\frac{1}{1+r}</math> and <math>v(x) = x\,f(x)^\frac{r}{1+r}</math> on a grid of values of <math>x</math>. Then, one can draw uniform samples <math>(u, v)\in \tilde{A}_{f,r}</math>, only keep those that fall inside the set <math>A_{f,r}</math> and return them as <math>\frac{v}{u^r}</math>.

It is possible to optimize the acceptance ratio by adjusting the value of <math>r</math>, as seen on the graphs.

== Software ==

* rust<ref>{{Citation | last= Northrop | first= P. J. | title= rust: Ratio-of-Uniforms Simulation with Transformation | year= 2021 | url= https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rust}}</ref> and Runuran<ref>{{Citation | first1= J. | last1= Leydold| first2= W. | last2= Hörmann| title= Runuran: R Interface to the 'UNU.RAN' Random Variate Generators | year= 2021 | url= https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=Runuran}}</ref> for multi-dimensional sampling in [[R (programming language)|R]]. 
* RatioUniforms and SROU within scipy.stats<ref>{{Cite web |title=Statistics (scipy.stats) — SciPy v1.16.2 Manual |url=https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy-1.16.2/tutorial/stats.html |access-date=2025-09-22 |website=docs.scipy.org}}</ref> for one-dimensional sampling in [[Python (programming language)|Python]]. 
* RUSampling<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jewson |first=L |date=2025 |title=RUSampling: Ratio-of-Uniforms sampling in Python |url=https://pypi.org/project/rusampling/ }}</ref> for multiple-dimension sampling in [[Python (programming language)|Python]].
